Title: The Origin and Practice of Yoga

Yoga began in ancient India thousands of years ago, even before any religion. Shiva, believed to be the first yogi and guru, passed his knowledge to seven sages, who carried it to many parts of the world, though India kept it in its fullest form. Remains of the Indus-Saraswati civilisation, folk traditions and Buddhist and Jain traditions show that yoga was practised in ancient India under a guru, with great stress on its spiritual value. Sun worship in the Vedic age later gave rise to Suryanamaskar. Maharishi Patanjali, the father of modern yoga, did not invent it but arranged its many forms into one system, the Yoga Sutras. Breath is central to yoga: asanas are done with slow movements and smooth, relaxed breathing.
answers.finalAnswer: Yoga began in ancient India, spread through Shiva's seven sages, was practised under gurus as shown by Indus-Saraswati remains, was organised by Patanjali in the Yoga Sutras, and centres on smooth breathing.

Essays written on (a) and (b).

(a) The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins with a Single Step

This wise saying of the Chinese thinker Lao Tzu means that even the biggest task begins with one small action. Many people dream of great goals but never start, because the goal looks too far away. A thousand miles cannot be covered in one jump, but they can be covered step by step. A student who wants to become an officer in the Army must begin today by studying one chapter well and running one extra round of the field. Mount Everest, too, was climbed one step at a time. Small steps taken every day add up to great success. So we should not wait for the perfect moment. We should take the first step now and keep walking with patience and courage.

(b) Need to Educate the Girl Child

It is said that if you educate a man, you educate one person, but if you educate a woman, you educate a whole family. Yet in many parts of our country, girls are still kept at home to do housework or are married off early. This is a great injustice. An educated girl can earn her living, stand on her own feet and make her own decisions. She looks after the health and studies of her children better. Educated women like Kalpana Chawla and Kiran Bedi have made the nation proud. The government has started schemes like 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao' to help girls go to school. But laws alone are not enough. Parents must give their daughters the same chances as their sons. Only then will India truly progress.

A Costly Lesson

Ravi, a young boy, was travelling by train to Delhi with a briefcase full of money. His father had asked him to deposit it in the bank. A smart, friendly man sat opposite him. He shared his food, told jokes and soon became Ravi's friend. Ravi told him about the money. When the train stopped at a station, Ravi felt hungry. 'Go and buy some snacks,' said the man. 'I will look after your briefcase.' Ravi went out happily. When he came back, both the man and the briefcase had disappeared. Ravi cried and reported the matter to the railway police, but the thief was never found. Ravi learnt a bitter lesson: never trust a stranger.

Compositions written on (a) and (c).

(a) Failures Are the Stepping Stones to Success

Failure is not the opposite of success; it is a part of it. Every failure teaches us a lesson and shows us where we went wrong. A child learning to walk falls many times before he can run. Thomas Edison tried hundreds of materials before he made a working electric bulb. He said that he had not failed, but had only found many ways that did not work. Abraham Lincoln lost several elections before he became President of America. Such people did not lose heart. They learnt from each failure and tried again with greater effort. We too should not be afraid of failing in a test or a game. If we learn from our mistakes and keep trying, each failure becomes a step on the ladder to success.

(c) Time and Tide Wait for None

Time is the most precious thing in life, because once it is gone, it never comes back. The tide of the sea does not wait for anyone, and neither does time. Lost money can be earned again and lost health can be regained with care, but lost time is lost forever. A student who wastes his days in idle talk, mobile games and television repents at examination time. A soldier who is late by even a minute may lose a battle. All great men valued every minute of their lives. We should make a timetable, do our work on time and never put off till tomorrow what we can do today. Those who respect time are respected by time.

The Editor
The Times of India
New Delhi

Subject: Students distracted by Facebook and WhatsApp

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to express my concern about how Facebook and WhatsApp are distracting students from their studies.

Today almost every student has a smartphone. Many of them spend hours chatting, sharing pictures and watching videos late into the night. Every few minutes a new message pulls them away from their books. As a result, they cannot concentrate, they sleep less and their marks fall. Some even get addicted and lose interest in games, reading and family life. Fake news and harmful content on these sites also mislead young minds.

Social media is not bad in itself; it can help us share notes and learn new things. But it must be used wisely. Parents should keep an eye on their children's screen time, schools should teach students about the safe and limited use of the internet, and students themselves should keep their phones away while studying.

I hope this letter will make students and parents think about this serious problem.

Yours faithfully
XYZ

The Necessity of Sanitation

Good morning respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends.

Today I want to speak on a subject that touches all our lives: the need for sanitation.

Walk through our town and you will see heaps of garbage by the roadside, open drains full of dirty water and people spitting and littering everywhere. These insanitary conditions are not just ugly; they are dangerous. Flies and mosquitoes breed in filth and spread diseases like cholera, typhoid, dengue and malaria. Every year thousands of children fall ill and many die because of dirty water and unclean surroundings.

Sanitation means keeping our homes, streets and water clean, using toilets and disposing of waste properly. It is not the job of the municipality alone. Each of us must do our part. Let us use dustbins, separate wet and dry waste, wash our hands before eating and never throw rubbish in the open. Let us also tell our families and neighbours to do the same.

We have all heard that cleanliness is next to godliness. If every citizen takes this pledge, our town will become clean, healthy and beautiful.

Thank you.
